name: TPS54560BDDAR
title: 60 V, 5 A buck converter with Eco-mode light-load skipping
summary: A 60 V, 5 A non-synchronous buck regulator with a 92 mΩ high-side MOSFET inside and an external Schottky catch diode. Peak current-mode control with external compensation runs at a fixed 100 kHz to 2.5 MHz, set by resistor or locked to a clock. Light loads are handled by pulse skipping, bringing the no-load draw to 146 µA; with EN low it falls to 2 µA. Protection covers cycle-by-cycle current limit, frequency foldback, output overvoltage and thermal shutdown, in an 8-pin HSOIC with exposed pad.
key_figures: 100 kHz to 2500 kHz (RT), 160 kHz to 2300 kHz (sync)

pins.name: BOOT
pins.function: Supply for the high-side gate driver. A capacitor connects BOOT to SW; if its voltage sags below what the switch needs, the switch is held off until the capacitor has been recharged.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Power input, 4.5 V to 60 V in operation.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable. An internal current source pulls it up, so left open the part runs; below 1.2 V it is off. Two resistors from VIN set a higher input undervoltage lockout.

pins.name: RT/CLK
pins.function: Frequency set. With a resistor to ground an internal amplifier holds the pin at a fixed voltage and the resistor sets the switching frequency. Driven above the PLL upper threshold, the amplifier turns off and the pin becomes a high-impedance clock input to the PLL; when the clock edges stop, the amplifier comes back and the resistor again sets the frequency.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback: the inverting input of the gm error amplifier.

pins.name: COMP
pins.function: Error amplifier output, which also sets the trip point of the PWM (switch current) comparator. The loop compensation network connects to this pin.

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Switch node, at the high-side MOSFET source.

pins.name: PWRPD
pins.function: Exposed thermal pad (PowerPAD). It must be joined on the board to the GND pin for the part to work properly.

circuits.title: 5 V output design example
circuits.description: A 400 kHz buck converter taking 7 V to 60 V down to 5 V at up to 5 A. Four 2.2 µF ceramics decouple the input. R1 and R2 on EN raise the input lockout so the part starts at 6.5 V and stops at 5 V. R3 sets the switching frequency. C4 is the bootstrap capacitor from BOOT to SW, and D1 is the Schottky catch diode from SW to ground that carries the inductor current while the switch is off. L1 and three 47 µF ceramics filter the output. R5 and R6 divide the output down to the 0.8 V reference on FB. On COMP, R4 with C5 sets the compensation zero and C8 adds a high-frequency pole.

circuits.title: Inverting power supply
circuits.description: The part makes a negative output from a positive input. Its GND pin, and with it the compensation, timing and feedback returns, sits on the negative output rail, while the inductor runs from SW to system ground. The catch diode goes from the negative rail to SW. R1 and R2 divide between system ground and the negative rail onto FB. Cin sits between VIN and system ground; Cd decouples VIN to the IC's GND. EN is left unconnected.

circuits.title: Split-rail power supply
circuits.description: A coupled inductor gives a positive and a negative output from one positive input. As in the inverting circuit, the IC's GND is the negative rail and the main winding runs from SW to system ground, with D1 from the negative rail to SW. The second winding, through D2, charges Copos to make the positive rail. R1 and R2 divide between the positive and negative rails onto FB. EN is left unconnected.

parts.note: coupled inductor; pins 1 and 4 are the dotted ends

notes: T1 pins: 1 to 2 is the winding between SW and ground, 3 to 4 the winding feeding D2.

equations.name: Minimum input voltage
equations.expr: VIN(min) = (VOUT + VF + Rdc × IOUT) / 0.99 + RDS(on) × IOUT − VF

where.VF: forward voltage of the Schottky catch diode
where.Rdc: DC resistance of the inductor plus board

equations.note: Use worst-case component values at the highest operating temperature.

equations.name: Maximum output voltage at heavy load (monotonic start-up)
equations.expr: VOUT(max) = D(max) × (VIN(min) − IOUT(max) × RDS(on) + VF) − VF + IOUT(max) × Rdc
equations.note: The IC clamps VBOOT; if the formula gives more than 6 V, take VBOOT = 6 V.

where.VSTART: input voltage at which switching starts
where.VSTOP: input voltage at which switching stops

equations.name: Switching frequency from RT
equations.note: A second form of the same fit uses 92471 in place of 92417: ƒsw (kHz) = 92471 × RT (kΩ)^-0.991.

equations.name: Highest frequency without pulse skipping
equations.expr: fSW(maxskip) = (1 / tON) × (IO × Rdc + VOUT + Vd) / (VIN − IO × RDS(on) + Vd)

equations.name: Highest frequency that frequency foldback still protects
equations.expr: fSW(shift) = (fDIV / tON) × (ICL × Rdc + VOUT(sc) + Vd) / (VIN − ICL × RDS(on) + Vd)

where.VOUT(sc): output voltage with the output shorted

equations.name: Control-to-output transfer function
equations.expr: VOUT / VC = Adc × (1 + s / (2π × fZ)) / (1 + s / (2π × fP))

equations.name: Minimum inductance
equations.expr: LO(min) = (VIN(max) − VOUT) / (IOUT × KIND) × VOUT / (VIN(max) × fSW) = (60 V − 5 V) / (5 A × 0.3) × 5 V / (60 V × 400 kHz) = 7.6 µH

where.KIND: inductor ripple current as a fraction of the maximum output current

equations.name: Inductor ripple current
equations.expr: IRIPPLE = VOUT × (VIN(max) − VOUT) / (VIN(max) × LO × fSW) = 5 V × (60 V − 5 V) / (60 V × 7.2 µH × 400 kHz) = 1.591 A

equations.name: Inductor peak current
equations.expr: IL(peak) = IOUT + IRIPPLE / 2 = 5 A + 1.591 A / 2 = 5.797 A

equations.name: Output capacitance for a load step
equations.expr: COUT > 2 × ΔIOUT / (fSW × ΔVOUT) = 2 × 2.5 A / (400 kHz × 0.2 V) = 62.5 µF

equations.name: Output capacitance for load release overshoot
equations.expr: COUT > LO × (IOH² − IOL²) / (Vf² − VI²) = 7.2 µH × (3.75² − 1.25²) A² / (5.2² − 5²) V² = 44.1 µF

equations.name: Output capacitance for ripple
equations.expr: COUT > (1 / (8 × fSW)) × 1 / (VORIPPLE / IRIPPLE) = (1 / (8 × 400 kHz)) × 1 / (25 mV / 1.591 A) = 19.9 µF

equations.name: Maximum output capacitor ESR
equations.expr: RESR < VORIPPLE / IRIPPLE = 25 mV / 1.591 A = 15.7 mΩ

equations.name: Output capacitor RMS ripple current
equations.expr: ICOUT(rms) = VOUT × (VIN(max) − VOUT) / (√12 × VIN(max) × LO × fSW) = 459 mA

equations.name: Catch diode power
equations.expr: PD = (VIN(max) − VOUT) × IOUT × Vfd / VIN(max) + Cj × fSW × (VIN + Vfd)² / 2 = (60 V − 5 V) × 5 A × 0.7 V / 60 V + 300 pF × 400 kHz × (60 V + 0.7 V)² / 2 = 3.43 W

equations.name: Input capacitor RMS current
equations.expr: ICI(rms) = IOUT × √(VOUT / VIN(min) × (VIN(min) − VOUT) / VIN(min)) = 5 A × √(5 V / 7 V × (7 V − 5 V) / 7 V) = 2.26 A

equations.name: Input ripple voltage
equations.expr: ΔVIN = IOUT × 0.25 / (CIN × fSW) = 5 A × 0.25 / (8.8 µF × 400 kHz) = 355 mV

equations.name: Modulator pole (design)
equations.expr: fP(mod) = IOUT(max) / (2π × VOUT × COUT) = 5 A / (2π × 5 V × 87.4 µF) = 1821 Hz

equations.name: ESR zero (design)
equations.expr: fZ(mod) = 1 / (2π × RESR × COUT) = 1 / (2π × 1.67 mΩ × 87.4 µF) = 1100 kHz

equations.name: Compensation resistor
equations.expr: R4 = (2π × fco × COUT / gmps) × (VOUT / (VREF × gmea)) = (2π × 29.2 kHz × 87.4 µF / 17 A/V) × (5 V / (0.8 V × 350 µA/V)) = 16.8 kΩ

equations.name: Compensation pole capacitor (ESR)
equations.expr: C8 = COUT × RESR / R4 = 87.4 µF × 1.67 mΩ / 16.9 kΩ = 8.64 pF

equations.name: Compensation pole capacitor (switching frequency)
equations.note: The larger of the two C8 results is used.

equations.name: Conduction loss
equations.expr: PCOND = IOUT² × RDS(on) × VOUT / VIN = 5 A² × 92 mΩ × 5 V / 12 V = 0.958 W

equations.name: Switching loss
equations.expr: PSW = VIN × fSW × IOUT × trise = 12 V × 400 kHz × 5 A × 4.9 ns = 0.118 W

where.trise: SW rise time, about VIN × 0.16 ns/V + 3 ns

equations.name: Gate drive loss
equations.expr: PGD = VIN × QG × fSW = 12 V × 3 nC × 400 kHz = 0.014 W

where.QG: gate charge of the integrated MOSFET

equations.name: Supply current loss
equations.expr: PQ = VIN × IQ = 12 V × 146 µA = 0.0018 W

equations.name: Total IC loss
equations.note: The loss equations hold in CCM only.

operation.text: Non-synchronous step-down (buck) converter, one channel, rated 60 V in and 5 A out, with a 92 mΩ n-channel high-side MOSFET inside and the catch diode outside. Control is fixed-frequency peak current mode with compensation on COMP, set anywhere from 100 kHz to 2.5 MHz by a resistor on RT/CLK or locked to an outside clock by an internal PLL. The 8-pin HSOIC has an exposed pad.
One orderable family, TPS54560BDDA (tube) and TPS54560BDDAR (reel), in the DDA package, marked 54560C. An automotive Q100 version is a separate part, the TPS54560B-Q1.
With no load and no switching the part draws 146 µA from VIN; pulled off by EN it draws 2 µA. The 5 V design example draws 257 µA from a 12 V input at no load.

Each cycle the oscillator turns the high-side switch on; it turns off when the sensed switch current reaches the level set by the COMP voltage, so COMP rises and falls with load. A clamp on the top of COMP sets the current limit, and a clamp at the bottom sets where pulse skipping begins. A ramp added to the sensed current stops subharmonic oscillation above 50 % duty; it does not lower the peak current limit at any duty cycle.

At light load, when the output is regulated and a cycle ends with a peak switch current below the skip threshold (the current that matches about 600 mV on COMP), switching halts and COMP is held at 600 mV. The output sags, COMP climbs, and switching resumes when COMP goes back over the threshold. The PLL keeps running, so skipped bursts stay aligned to an outside clock. The device watches peak switch current, not load current, so the load at which it starts skipping depends on the inductor: about 25.3 mA in the 5 V example, which enters DCM below 408 mA at 12 V in.

A 0.1 µF ceramic, X5R or X7R, 10 V or more, from BOOT to SW drives the high-side gate; the recharge diode is inside. It recharges while the switch is off and the catch diode conducts. The switch may stay on at 100 % duty as long as BOOT-SW is above 2.1 V; below that it is turned off and a small internal low-side MOSFET pulls SW down to recharge the capacitor. This low-side MOSFET is turned off when the output reaches 24 V and back on when the output falls to 21.5 V. Since the gate draws little charge the switch can stay on for many cycles, so the duty cycle in dropout approaches 100 %, limited by switch, inductor, diode and board drops (Equation 1).

A transconductance amplifier compares FB with whichever is lower, the soft-start ramp or the 0.8 V reference. Its gm is 350 µA/V in normal operation and drops to about 78 µA/V during soft start. Compensation parts go from COMP to GND.

A divider from the output to FB sets the output against the 0.8 V reference, which holds ±1 % over temperature and supply. Divider resistors of 1 % or better are recommended. Larger values save light-load current but make FB more sensitive to noise and to its input current; in the example the divider current is kept above 1 µA, which holds as long as the lower resistor is under 800 kΩ. The lowest output is 0.8 V; the highest is close to the lowest input.

The part runs once VIN is above 4.3 V and EN is above 1.2 V, and stops when VIN drops under 4 V or EN goes below 1.2 V. A 1.2 µA source pulls EN up, so the pin may float. Once EN is above the threshold, a further 3.4 µA flows out of the pin, and it is removed again when EN falls below; with a divider from VIN this current gives the input lockout an adjustable hysteresis (Equations 4 and 5). Where a low start voltage meets a high input, EN can be driven past its 8.4 V rating; a zener clamp on EN is recommended then. Below 4.5 V in the part may still run down to its lockout, but operation above 4.5 V is recommended.

A digital soft start raises the reference from 0 V to 0.8 V over 1024 switching cycles (Equation 6): 2.1 ms at 500 kHz, 0.42 ms at 2.5 MHz. It resets when EN goes low, in thermal shutdown, and on an overload; after an overload clears, soft start controls the climb back to regulation.

A resistor from RT/CLK to GND, placed close to the IC with short traces because the pin picks up noise, sets 100 kHz to 2500 kHz (Equations 7 and 8); the pin sits at about 0.5 V. A typical 135 ns minimum on-time caps the frequency at high step-down ratios (Equation 9); frequency foldback sets a second cap (Equation 10). In the 5 V example these give 708 kHz and 855 kHz and 400 kHz is used.

The switch current limit is accurate, with a typical delay of 60 ns, so a small inductor lets the peak inductor current overshoot the limit by VIN / L × the delay. To keep the inductor current under control in a short, the clock is cut to 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 as FB drops from 0.8 V toward 0 V, and the longer off-time lets the current fall. Foldback is digital, so it works with an outside clock too.

RT/CLK accepts a square wave that goes below 0.5 V and above 1.7 V with pulses over 15 ns, from 160 kHz to 2300 kHz; each falling clock edge starts a rising SW edge. The first time the pin is driven above the PLL threshold, the 0.5 V source is removed, the pin goes high impedance and the PLL locks within 78 µs. The frequency resistor should still pull RT/CLK to ground when the clock stops. With a low-impedance source, RT runs from the pin to a termination resistor (for example 50 Ω) to ground, the clock drives their junction, and a capacitor across RT couples the clock to the pin; the two resistors in series should set close to the clock frequency; AC coupling through a 10 pF ceramic is recommended. When the clock is lost the frequency drops to 150 kHz and then moves to the resistor-set value.

If FB rises above 109 % of the reference, the high-side switch is shut off at once; it resumes when FB falls under 106 %. This limits overshoot when an overload is released or the load drops quickly with a small output capacitor.
Above a junction temperature of 176 °C the switch stops. Below 164 °C the part restarts through soft start.

For CCM the power stage acts as a current source of 17 A/V from COMP into the output capacitor and load, giving one dominant pole that moves with load (so crossover stays put) and an ESR zero (Equations 11 to 14). The error amplifier is a 350 µA/V transconductance stage whose gain and bandwidth are modelled by Ro and Co. Type 2A, 2B and Type 1 networks are supported: Type 2 for low-ESR output capacitors, Type 1 for high-ESR electrolytic or tantalum (Equations 15 to 24).

A ripple ratio KIND of up to 0.3 suits low-ESR ceramics; about 0.2 suits higher-ESR capacitors. The inductor ripple current must stay above 150 mA for stable PWM. On a wide input range a larger ripple keeps enough ripple at minimum input. The inductor's RMS and saturation ratings must not be exceeded; the most conservative choice rates saturation at or above the switch current limit, nominally 7.5 A.

Size it by the strictest of three needs: holding the output through a load step for about two clock cycles (Equation 32), absorbing the inductor energy on a load release since the diode cannot sink current (Equation 33), and the ripple limit (Equations 34 and 35). Derate ceramics for DC bias, temperature and age; electrolytic and tantalum ESR must enter the load-step sums. Check the RMS ripple current rating (Equation 36).

A diode from SW to GND is required. Its reverse rating must be at least the maximum input, preferably 60 V, and its peak current rating above the maximum inductor current. Schottky types suit it for their low forward drop. Its losses include conduction during the off-time and, at high frequency, junction capacitance and recovery charge (Equation 37). For long periods at light load, a diode with lower leakage and a little more forward drop can be better.

At least 3 µF of effective ceramic capacitance, X5R or X7R, after DC-bias loss, rated above the maximum input voltage and for the input ripple current (Equation 38). Bulk capacitance may be added. If the source is more than a few inches away, extra bulk capacitance, typically a 100 µF electrolytic, may be needed.

Derating curves show the ambient temperatures at which internal and external parts stay at or under their rated temperatures, measured on a double-sided board with 2 oz copper. In most conditions the catch diode limits first; at high duty cycle or high switching frequency the IC can become the limit.

Bypass VIN to ground with a low-ESR X5R or X7R ceramic, keeping small the loop through that capacitor, VIN and the catch diode's anode. Tie GND straight to the exposed pad and stitch the pad to inner ground planes with several vias under the IC. Run SW to the diode cathode and the inductor, keep those parts close and the SW copper small to cut capacitive coupling. At full load, top-side ground copper also has to spread the heat. Keep the RT resistor right at the pin. The 5 V design example takes about 1.025 in² (661 mm²) of board, without test points or connectors.

With its ground pin tied to the negative output the part can make a negative rail from a positive input, for example for amplifiers; with a coupled inductor it can make a positive and a negative rail at once.
